entry.d: Augustine of Hippo (354–430) was a restless African teacher who found God after years of wandering. As bishop of Hippo he shepherded his people, defended the faith, and left the Confessions and The City of God.

sections.b:
Augustine was born on November 13, 354, at Tagaste, a small city of Numidia in North Africa. His father, Patricius, sat on the town council and was still a pagan. His mother, Monica, was a Christian whose virtues, the sources say, at last won her husband to baptism.

As a child Augustine was signed with the cross and enrolled among the catechumens. Once, gravely ill, he asked for baptism, but he recovered and the sacrament was put off, as was common then. Yet the name of the Savior, he tells us, had been drawn in with his mother's milk, and nothing without it could wholly win him. In this boy we meet the mystery of a heart claimed by God long before it knows how to answer.

Patricius wished his gifted son to study at Carthage, but the money took months to gather. Augustine spent his sixteenth year at home in idleness, and by his own account he gave himself over to pleasure. He reached Carthage near the end of 370, and the great city drew him further from his course. He formed a liaison with a woman who bore him a son, Adeodatus. In 373 he read Cicero's Hortensius, and a love of wisdom woke in him. Yet his faith went astray. For nine years he followed the Manichaeans, though he never rose above the rank of "auditor." When their celebrated bishop Faustus came to Carthage, he could not answer Augustine's questions, and the spell was broken. All the while Monica prayed. A bishop consoled her with the assurance that "the son of so many tears could not perish."

In 383 Augustine left for Rome, slipping away by night because Monica did not want to be parted from him. He then won a teaching post at Milan, where he began to attend the preaching of Bishop Ambrose. Three years of struggle followed. He read Plato and Plotinus, and he turned to the Scriptures, especially the letters of St. Paul. Still his will held back. Then a visitor named Pontitian spoke of the life of St. Antony, and Augustine saw his own hesitation plainly. In the Confessions he tells us that he went into a garden and cried out to the Lord. He heard a child's voice repeating the words tolle lege, take and read. He opened St. Paul's letters at random, read the first passage he saw, and felt his long struggle end. This was September 386.

Augustine resigned his professorship and withdrew with Monica, Adeodatus, and friends to the country estate of Verecundus at Cassisiacum. At Easter in 387 Ambrose baptized him at Milan, together with Adeodatus and Alypius. The friends then set out for Africa. At Ostia, in the autumn of 387, Monica died, and Augustine gave some of the most moving pages of the Confessions to her memory. He later returned to Tagaste. There he sold his goods for the poor and lived in common with friends in poverty, prayer, and study. Soon grief came again, for the gifted Adeodatus died at seventeen.

Augustine had no wish to be a priest and avoided cities where a bishop was being chosen. In 391, at Hippo, he was praying in church when the people crowded round him and begged Bishop Valerius to ordain him. With tears he yielded. Valerius set aside church property for a monastery and had him preach, though in Africa that task usually belonged to bishops.

In 396, at forty-two, he was consecrated to assist the aging Valerius, and he held the see for thirty-four years. His house became a community whose clergy gave up private property. His sister Perpetua led a community of religious women. A letter he wrote for them, with two sermons, makes up what is called the Rule of St. Augustine.

He was a shepherd as well as a thinker. "I do not wish to be saved without you," he told his people.

His preaching and letters reached far beyond Hippo. In 404 he met the Manichaean leader Felix in public conference, and Felix confessed the Catholic faith. Against the Donatists, whose schism had grown vast in Africa, he first sought friendly conference. When violence met these efforts, he came to approve firmer laws, yet he never wished heresy punished by death. When Alaric took Rome in 410, pagans blamed the abandoned gods. In answer Augustine began The City of God in 413, and he finished it in 426. Against Pelagius, who denied original sin, a council at Carthage condemned the Pelagians in 412, and Pope Zosimus did so in 418. Augustine held that we depend wholly on God for salvation. In his seventy-second year he reviewed his own writings in the Retractations, correcting errors with candor. In 426 he had the deacon Heraclius acclaimed as his successor.

The last years were darkened by the Vandals, who landed in Africa in May 428. Towards the end of May 430 they appeared before Hippo. That summer Augustine fell ill of a fever that he knew would be fatal. He spoke of death with serene confidence in God's mercy, and he asked that the penitential psalms be written out and hung on the wall by his bed. He died on August 28, 430, at the age of seventy-five, with his mind clear to the end. What does he say to us now? That no one is too far gone for God. In the Confessions he cries: "Too late have I loved Thee, O Beauty so old and so new! Too late have I loved Thee." In our own restless seasons we hear in these words a man found by the One he sought. And his City of God still bears witness that history belongs to the Lord.

reviewNotes.note: Left out on purpose because the sources disagree: Augustine's age at conversion (33 in source 1, 32 in source 2), the length of the siege of Hippo (18 months in source 1, 14 in source 2), and years as bishop (34 or 35). The sources name no modern country; "Algeria" in the country field comes from outside them and needs confirmation.
Canonization and patronage are not given by the sources. Source 2's claim that he was canonized under Pope Leo I is not repeated. The Te Deum baptism legend is dismissed by source 1 and was omitted.
